resources.string: How the parathyroid glands regulate calcium

A qualitative view of normal human calcium feedback, focused on the parathyroid glands, kidneys, and small intestine. Timing, particle counts, and anatomy are schematic, not measurements or predictions.
Chief cells sense lower ionized calcium
Calcium-sensing receptors on parathyroid chief cells respond to free (ionized) calcium outside the cells. As ionized calcium falls, the receptors are less active.
When calcium-sensing receptor activity falls, chief cells release more parathyroid hormone (PTH). The hormone enters nearby capillaries and travels through the blood.
The kidneys retain calcium and activate vitamin D
PTH helps the kidneys return more calcium from tubule fluid to the blood. It separately promotes formation of active vitamin D in the kidneys.
Active vitamin D supports intestinal calcium uptake
Active vitamin D helps cells lining the small intestine absorb calcium from the lumen into the blood. This effect of PTH is indirect, through active vitamin D.
PTH release eases as calcium recovers
As ionized calcium recovers, calcium-sensing receptors become more active again. Chief cells release less PTH, easing the response that helped restore calcium.
Evidence: the human parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor
Evidence: parathyroid regulation of vitamin D activation in rats
